title: Insurer-Billable Circles for GLP-1 Quitters
one_liner: Twelve-week therapist-and-dietitian-led groups for people coming off GLP-1s, funded through behavioral-health and nutrition benefits rather than 'weight loss' budgets.
customer: Employers and carriers that just dropped GLP-1 coverage (about 14% more plan to by 2027) and the ex-users themselves ($299 cash cohorts to start). GLP-1 telehealth firms are a later channel, as a retention add-on.
problem: Only about a third of non-diabetic patients are still on therapy at 1 year, and cost is the top reason. Stoppers regain weight about 4x faster than behavioral losers, roughly 60% of ex-users intend to restart, and 70% report lost joy in eating. Returning food noise, binge eating and body-identity distress get no clinical owner, because pharma, PBMs and telehealth are paid for volume or price, not persistence.
solution: Small cohorts of about 8 are co-led by a licensed therapist (CBT/ACT, binge-eating experience) and a registered dietitian. Content covers returning food noise, structured eating, protein and resistance-training basics, and a relapse plan. A partner prescriber offers a taper or low-cost maintenance plan (for example a $149 pill) and defines restart triggers. Where clinically indicated (BED, adjustment disorder), sessions bill as in-network group psychotherapy (CPT 90853) with dietitian MNT, using honest coding only. Employers can instead buy it as a $450-700 per-participant 'transition benefit'.
why_now: Employer GLP-1 coverage for weight loss fell from 72% to 60% in 2026 and more employers are dropping it before open enrollment now. Brand pill prices fell to $149-$299 cash, so 'restart cheaply' is a real option. The Medicare $50 Bridge copay ends Dec 2027, and JAMA Psychiatry 2026 found GLP-1 use of about 50% among binge-eating-disorder patients.
revenue_model: In-network group-therapy and MNT claims, or an employer per-participant fee ($450-700 per 12-week cohort versus about $12k a year for the drug), plus an optional $29-49 per month prescriber maintenance subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Employers cut coverage to save money and created a pool of abrupt discontinuers with no plan. The only bundle in this space that insurers already pay for by law is behavioral-health group care, so the funding path is mental-health parity, not obesity medicine. That also aligns with the psychological cause of regain (food noise, identity, bingeing) rather than another diet.
first_30_days: Sign one therapist with binge-eating experience and one RD, both credentialed through an existing group practice. Recruit the first cohort of 8 from GLP-1 subreddits and Facebook groups at $299 cash. Approach three mid-size employers through brokers who have just announced dropped coverage. Track 12-week weight regain, binge episodes and restart rates against a naive expectation.

title: Scam-Compound Geo-Intelligence for Compliance Teams
one_liner: A monthly geospatial register of scam compounds, built from satellite imagery and RF data, that lets exchanges and banks flag payees and merchants with a physical nexus to them.
customer: Financial-crime investigators and sanctions teams at crypto exchanges, stablecoin off-ramps, OTC desks, Asian correspondent banks and payment processors. Secondary: anti-scam consortia (for example GASA members) and the US/UK scam-center task forces that agreed on 4 Sept 2026 to coordinate takedowns.
problem: Chainalysis puts 2025 scam revenue near $17B, with AI-enabled operations averaging $3.2M versus $719K, and US investment fraud alone hit $8.65B. On-chain tools label wallets but nobody maps the physical compounds (Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos, now spreading) to counterparties. Compounds relocate after raids, and enforcement and sanctions need evidence of place, not just of transactions.
solution: A register of suspected compounds and displacement corridors built from optical and SAR change detection (perimeter walls, dormitory blocks, razor-wire, rooftop dish counts, nighttime lights) plus purchased RF-geolocation data on satellite-terminal uplinks, cross-referenced to corporate registries and Telegram guarantee marketplaces. Delivered as a risk API and CSV: 'this payee's declared address, IP cluster or KYC address is within X km of a flagged compound', with analyst-reviewed confidence tiers and evidence packets for suspicious-activity reports. Also a relocation forecast near border economic zones.
why_now: The US and UK agreed on 4 Sept 2026 to coordinate scam-center takedowns, and 2025 sanctions on the Prince Group showed enforcement appetite. Commercial revisit rates and cheap SAR now make monthly monitoring affordable. Reporting has documented satellite-internet terminals at compounds, giving them an RF and imagery signature.
revenue_model: $3-8K per compound-exposure assessment for investigations teams and $10-25K per month for the risk feed and API. Consortium data-sharing licences later.
non_obvious_insight: On-chain analytics see money but not place, and compounds are physically huge, slow to build and hard to hide, unlike wallets. They sit in a gap between defense-intel EO buyers and commercial AML, so no one serves them. Compliance teams need geographic-nexus evidence to justify de-risking specific corridors instead of blanket bans, and a place-based register gives regulators something to point to.
first_30_days: Validate signatures on known compounds (KK Park, Shwe Kokko, Sihanoukville, Golden Triangle zone) with Sentinel-1 and 2 plus $5-10K of commercial imagery credit. Publish a free 'Compound Atlas' of 30 sites with human-reviewed confidence tiers. Pitch 5 exchange investigations heads and one anti-scam NGO consortium, and sell 2-3 paid assessments.

title: Battery-Islanded Feeders Instead of Undergrounding
one_liner: Sell utilities islandable rural feeders powered by enrolled home batteries as a cheaper alternative to undergrounding and repeated wildfire power shutoffs.
customer: Wildfire-exposed utilities and co-ops (California, Pacific Northwest, Colorado, Hawaii), funded from wildfire-mitigation capex. Tribal and community microgrids are a secondary buyer.
problem: Undergrounding costs roughly $2-3M or more per mile, and public safety power shutoffs cut power to thousands of homes for days. Home batteries are common (46% storage attach), but each only serves its own house, and utilities cannot use them to keep a whole feeder alive.
solution: A feeder-level controller, smart switch and grid-forming coordination software that lets a segment island when upstream is de-energized, with enrolled home batteries powering critical loads. The same software runs normal VPP dispatch to pay for itself. The utility contracts it as a non-wires wildfire alternative.
why_now: 140k batteries delivered 580 MW on Sept 9, grid-forming inverters are now standard, wildfire budgets are large, and affordability limits undergrounding.
revenue_model: $150-400 per customer-year availability payment from the utility, a controller lease, and VPP revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The battery is already in the house, and the missing pieces are coordination and a switch. Utilities cannot earn a return on efficiency, but they can on wildfire mitigation capex, and you are competing against $3M per mile.
first_30_days: Approach small co-ops and munis in fire-prone areas. Pick a 200-home feeder with at least 30% battery attach. Propose a paid $40k feasibility study and a pilot using existing devices. Partner with a microgrid-controller vendor.

title: Provider-in-Residence: Vacant Units Become Childcare
one_liner: Convert vacant ground-floor apartments in lease-up buildings into licensed family child care homes run by vetted early-educator residents, paid for out of the landlord's existing concession budget.
customer: Multifamily owners and operators in concession-heavy Sun Belt markets (success fee per activated unit), family child care entrepreneurs (a back-office subscription), and residents or subsidy programs paying tuition.
problem: Licensed capacity is barely growing (centers +1.5% and family homes +4.3% in 2024) while two children in center care cost more than rent in every state and the average childcare worker earns about $33,000. Meanwhile 1.2M apartment units are in lease-up, concessions run 15.8% of stabilized units (37% in Austin), it takes 34 days to lease, and owners are giving away free months on units that could earn nothing better.
solution: Pre-screen buildings for ground-floor 2-3 bedroom units that pass local family child care home rules (which in many states are treated as residential use). Recruit early educators, nannies and ex-teachers, fit out the unit (child-proofing, egress), coach them through licensing, and lease them the unit at a discount in place of the concession, so they live and work there. Resident families get priority. The operator handles enrollment, billing, subsidy paperwork, insurance and a shared substitute pool across buildings.
why_now: The lease-up glut has made concessions a real, measurable budget line and landlords are experimenting with anything that fills units or improves retention. The 2025-26 tax changes (DCFSA raised to $7,500, larger 45F credit) push employers and families toward childcare spending. Family child care homes are the fastest-growing licensed segment.
revenue_model: Landlord success fee of about $2-4K per activated unit (about one to two months of rent), 6-8% of tuition for back-office and subsidy handling, and a group insurance margin.
non_obvious_insight: A childcare seat is worth about $1,300 a month to a family, far more than a month of free rent is to a prospect, and a family with a child in the building is far less likely to move. The concession budget is already spent, and spending it on seats produces supply in a category where zoning is usually on your side.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with high concessions such as Austin, Phoenix, Atlanta or Nashville and check the state's family-home rules (ratios, floor level, egress). Pitch 5 lease-up operators and sign two letters of intent for 2-3 units each. Recruit three providers through early-educator communities and begin licensing, aiming for first enrollments by month four or five.

title: Contingency-Fee Audit of OTA Markups and Payouts
one_liner: Mystery-shop every downstream reseller and reconcile every OTA payout, then take a share of the money and direct bookings recovered.
customer: Independent hotels of 20-200 rooms and small groups in Europe and the US paying 15-28% commissions.
problem: 51% of European hotels say OTAs sell below their loaded rate, up from 40% two years ago, and 26% do not know whether rates are passed on. Markups by Agoda, Citi, AA, Southwest and loyalty partners are invisible to rate-shopping tools. Hotels are paid after checkout, and commission, virtual-card fee and no-show errors go unchecked. In-house monitoring exists for chains (Radisson watches 1,600 properties), but independents have nothing.
solution: Combine automated and human shoppers that check rates across OTAs and reseller portals with screenshots per date, and reservation-level reconciliation of booked rate, commission, payout, card fees, cancellations and no-shows. Produce evidence packs to send to OTA account managers and a price-integrity dashboard that supports the case for direct booking.
why_now: Booking's payment service touched about 70% of its 2025 bookings, which concentrates the opacity. Google AI Overviews now reportedly show hotel prices and cut metasearch clicks, which pushes hotels to defend direct channels. Channel managers now expose reservation data.
revenue_model: 20-25% of recovered commission and no-show revenue, plus USD 99-299 per month for ongoing price-integrity monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: OTAs cannot audit themselves and hotels cannot see downstream markups, the same structural gap that made freight-bill and telecom-audit firms lucrative. The shopping evidence is the leverage in negotiations.
first_30_days: Offer 20 hotels a free 'leak report' covering 30 future dates, using human plus scripted shoppers. Convert the worst-leaking ones to contingency contracts, using hotel associations for introductions.

title: Compliance-First CDL School Roll-Up for Carriers
one_liner: Buy the clean CDL schools that survived the federal crackdown, run them with AI scheduling and audit-ready records, and get paid per hired graduate by carriers.
customer: Trucking carriers (pay-per-hire or tuition guarantees), students (financed), and workforce boards. School owners are the sellers.
problem: FMCSA removed nearly 3,000 providers from the Training Provider Registry and has thousands more under investigation. The non-domiciled CDL rule effective 16 March 2026 removed an estimated 90,000+ CDLs. Carriers need legitimate, US-domiciled drivers with provable training, and independent schools are mom-and-pop operations with thin documentation, idle trucks and scarce instructors.
solution: Acquire mid-size schools with clean records. AI ops: scheduling that keeps trucks and instructors busy, automatic ELDT and registry records with an audit-ready evidence packet per student, simulators and camera or telematics coaching that shorten range hours, and a placement engine matching graduates to carriers. Carriers pay a bounty per hire and back student financing.
why_now: The 2026 crackdown turned record quality into a scarce, acquirable asset, and capacity is tight. Carriers want vetted sources of drivers, and simulators and telematics are now cheap.
revenue_model: Tuition of $4k to $8k per student (self-pay, financed, or WIOA-funded), carrier placement fees of $3k to $6k per hire, and simulator licensing to smaller schools.
non_obvious_insight: After a regulatory purge, provenance is the product. The school that can prove every training hour becomes a carrier's preferred feeder farm, so audit-ready data is worth more than the trucks. Reputation risk from CDL mills is a barrier to entry for bad actors and a marketing asset for a clean operator.
first_30_days: Sign a letter of intent with one small school owner on seller financing. Sign two regional carriers to a pilot pay-per-hired-graduate agreement. Put cameras and telematics on two training trucks and produce a sample audit packet. Publish pass and placement data.

title: Result-Loop Desk for Scan and Lab Startups
one_liner: An outsourced nurse-and-radiologist desk that closes the loop on abnormal results from full-body scans, MCED tests and mega-panels.
customer: Mid-tier consumer diagnostics operators without downstream care: full-body MRI resellers, regional imaging centers, longevity clinics, mega-panel labs and employer executive-health programs.
problem: A review of 12 studies found 95% of asymptomatic people had at least one abnormal whole-body MRI finding and 91% of those were not clinically relevant (15-30% false-positive rate). Primary-care waits average ~31 days, so patients arrive at their PCP with printouts. Adoption is accelerating (Neko $700M for a NYC launch, Function 1M+ members), and Lp(a) testing hit a wall when Lp(a)HORIZON failed on Sep 4, 2026, leaving many flagged people without a next step.
solution: Triage each flagged result (ignore, repeat in X months, refer), track follow-up imaging against nodule and lesion guidelines, produce a structured PCP handoff (FHIR), document loop closure and route to a price-transparent cash referral network. Sold as a risk-management service. Consumers can buy a $99 second-opinion review.
why_now: Elective screening boomed in 2025-26 (Function-Ezra, Neko US launch, MCED tests despite NHS-Galleri missing its primary endpoint in May 2026). Medscape and radiology press now describe a 'medical cascade', so reputation and liability risk are becoming visible to operators.
revenue_model: $40-150 per flagged member (B2B), plus annual tracking fee per incidental finding, plus consumer second-opinion upsell.
non_obvious_insight: Screening companies are paid at the scan, but the costs of false positives and lost follow-ups land months later on nobody. Because they are not care providers, they cannot build the follow-up function in-house, so it converts to a compliance product.
first_30_days: Sell a pilot to three regional imaging centers or longevity clinics that resell whole-body MRI. Staff one part-time radiologist and one RN navigator, run follow-up tracking with SMS and a spreadsheet, and charge $75 per flagged patient. Publish a 'follow-up leakage' audit as the sales asset.

title: Cross-Mine Critical Spares Pool and Inventory Cleanup
one_liner: An AI cleaner for mine SAP materials masters that frees cash from duplicate spares, then turns the informal WhatsApp groups of competing mines' maintenance planners into a contractual, insured rotables pool for mill motors, liners and haul-truck parts.
customer: Supply chain, maintenance and finance heads at mid-size copper and lithium operations, starting in clusters where operators are neighbours: Arizona, Nevada and Utah, Antofagasta, the Arequipa-Moquegua corridor, the Zambian Copperbelt and the Pilbara. They pay a share of freed cash, not an IT budget.
problem: A copper mine holds $30-150M of spares. Materials masters are full of duplicates and near-duplicates (the same bearing under five descriptions), often 20-30% of items, so mines overbuy what is on another shelf. They still stock out on truly critical items (mill drive motors, girth gears, transformers, big castings) with 12-24 month lead times. Meanwhile maintenance planners across competing companies already borrow parts from each other over WhatsApp groups. It works only among friends and has no contracts, insurance, condition guarantees or return terms, so it never scales.
solution: Step one is the wedge. A CSV export of the SAP MM data goes into an LLM pipeline with OEM and aftermarket cross-references, multilingual description normalisation and criticality scoring. It outputs a list of duplicates, surplus and dead stock, plus the freed working capital in dollars. Step two lists surplus and 'insurance spares' on a members-only district board with a standard loan, lease and sale agreement, third-party condition inspection (vibration, NDT), logistics and insurance. It works like airline rotable pooling: three neighbouring mines share one spare mill motor instead of each stocking one.
why_now: Large motors, transformers and castings have longer lead times because of grid and data-centre demand. Steel and copper tariffs make replacement parts pricier. Lithium mines are cash-starved after the price bust, and copper mines face cost inflation and grade decline, so CFOs are hunting working capital. LLMs can now normalise messy multilingual part descriptions at almost no cost, which was not economic three years ago.
revenue_model: 15-25% of freed cash (sales and avoided purchases only, not write-offs), a pool membership subscription ($1-3k per month), and an 8-10% transaction fee on pooled loans and sales, plus inspection and certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: The spares problem is legal and trust-based, not a software problem. The informal swap network is the real supply chain. The biggest saving is not selling dead stock, it is not buying the 'insurance spare' a neighbour already owns. Pooling is an aviation idea that mining has never adopted because competitors will not share data without a neutral third party.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, offer a free 2-week scan of SAP MM exports (CSV) at two or three mid-size mines. Deliver a dollar value of duplicates and surplus and a target list. Sign a success-fee agreement with the first one that shows a big number. In parallel, seed a private 'list before you buy' board among 20 maintenance planners in one district using Signal or WhatsApp, to formalise the network before any software is built.

title: Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense
one_liner: A 48-hour, coder-certified benchmark report that tells defense lawyers and auto carriers what a letter-of-protection medical bill is actually worth.
customer: Insurance defense law firms and auto-carrier litigation/SIU units handling bodily-injury claims in tort-reform states (Florida, Georgia, Texas, Louisiana first). Volume firms pay per report. Carriers pay monthly.
problem: Plaintiff-side injury cases increasingly rest on treatment provided under letters of protection (LOP), where the provider is paid from the settlement and bills at a private rate card. Defense lawyers have to show what the care is really worth. Today that means a $3-5k billing expert, a slow turnaround, and a fight over methodology. Most claims examiners cannot read a CMS-1500 or UB-04, so inflated bills mostly get paid or settled at face value.
solution: Intake the itemized bill and records. Map every line to CPT/HCPCS and revenue codes and flag unbundling (e.g. 99215-25 plus separate injection administration, physician-owned ASC facility fees stacked on the professional fee, stacked imaging reads). Benchmark each line against Medicare multiples, hospital-posted commercial negotiated rates from price-transparency files, and local percentiles. The output is a Daubert-hardened PDF signed by a certified coder (CPC/CCS) with an optional expert declaration or testimony upsell. It is a methodology plus a template, so the marginal cost per report is about an hour of coder time.
why_now: Florida's 2023 tort reform made LOP arrangements discoverable and admitted evidence of amounts actually paid. Georgia's 2025 tort reform pushed similar rules, and other states are copying. Hospital price-transparency rules that took full effect in 2026 now require actual payment amounts where rates are percentages or algorithms, so a defensible local benchmark exists for the first time.
revenue_model: $295-$695 per report. Expert declaration or testimony at $1,500-$3,500. $2-5k/month subscriptions for carriers and volume firms with a report quota. Gross margin is high because coders are paid per report as contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Inside a hospital, chargemaster prices are understood to be fiction, and every biller knows what things really get paid. Injury lawyers have been arguing about 'reasonable value' without that insider map. Certified coders also know the tells of bills built for litigation rather than payment: modifier-25 patterns, unbundled facility fees, and E/M levels that no insurer would ever pay. The market is starved of people credentialed and willing to say so on paper. The moat is a coder bench plus a methodology that survives cross-examination, not software.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 CPC/CCS coders (ex-hospital, remote, contractors) and one defense-attorney advisor to review the methodology memo. Build the report template from the free Medicare fee schedules plus a few metro-area price-transparency files. Cold-email about 100 Florida and Georgia defense firms and claims managers, and offer 5 free reports on live cases in exchange for a methodology review and a testimonial. Convert the first 3-5 to $349 per report, then price the expert declaration as an add-on.

title: 90-Day Bridge Power for Robotaxi Depots
one_liner: Containerized battery-buffered charging stalls leased per stall per month so AV fleets can open depots years before the utility connects them.
customer: Robotaxi fleet operators and depot managers, autonomous-truck terminals, and electric delivery-van fleets that need charging capacity fast.
problem: Depot power is the scaling choke point. California lead times run about 6 months for a standard charging site, 1.9 years for a new circuit, 2.8 years for a substation upgrade and 8.9 years for a new substation, and depots compete with data centers for powered industrial land. Waymo alone has 3,871 vehicles and is aiming much higher.
solution: Modular systems combining second-life EV battery storage, a small grid tie (200-500 kW) and charging software that schedules vehicles around available energy. Sell 'stalls online in 90 days' as power-as-a-service. When the full grid connection arrives, the same assets convert to peak shaving and grid-services revenue.
why_now: Waymo, Tesla and Zoox (charging fares since August 10, 2026) are all scaling at once, and interconnection queues now outrun vehicle deployment. Data-center bridge power has proven that customers will pay a premium for time-to-power.
revenue_model: $600-1,000 per stall per month, or $0.30-0.45 per kWh delivered, on 3-5 year contracts, with asset financing behind them.
non_obvious_insight: For AV scale-up the binding constraint is interconnection time, not vehicles or software. Turning 'megawatts in two years' into 'kilowatts now, megawatts later' beats the utility's queue, and buffered assets keep earning after the grid arrives.
first_30_days: Get an LOI for a 20-stall pilot from one depot operator or delivery-van fleet. Source used battery modules through a reseller and integrate an existing containerized storage vendor's hardware rather than building your own. Target first revenue in month 4.

title: Knowledge Trusts That Pay Heirs From AI Licensing
one_liner: A fiduciary licensing shop that records a retiring or terminally ill master practitioner's judgment, holds the rights in an estate-friendly trust, sells non-exclusive licenses to AI buyers, and pays royalties to the expert and later the heirs.
customer: Two payers. First, employers and trade associations with an irreplaceable expert aged 62-75 about to retire, who pay for a knowledge-capture sprint. Second, AI labs, vertical AI vendors and professional-training firms that license the corpus. Beneficiaries are the expert and heirs. Channel: estate attorneys and wealth managers, who want an heir-engagement hook (Cerulli says 89% of firms treat family meetings as essential).
problem: The scarcest input for AI is long-tail, high-stakes tacit judgment (how a 40-year surety underwriter smells a bad bond, how a master electrician diagnoses an odd fault). It sits in the heads of people near retirement or death. Hourly expert-gig marketplaces pay by the hour with no royalties. They rarely reach 65+ specialists, and nobody structures who owns the recordings, annotations or persona rights after death, so it all falls into probate limbo. Meanwhile 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are about 19% below trend (Stanford) and have no path to learn from these people.
solution: 1) Structured elicitation: 30-40 hours of rubric-guided sessions (case walk-throughs, 'what would you do and why not that', annotated redacted real work). Junior apprentice-interviewers from the same field, meaning recent grads or displaced mid-career people, run them. They are paid and earn a verifiable co-credit. 2) Rights go into a knowledge trust drafted with the client's estate attorney: consent controls, approved-buyer list, sunset dates, and no voice, likeness or persona cloning unless explicitly opted in. 3) Non-exclusive licensing of the corpus to labs and enterprise vendors. Royalties go to the expert while alive and to heirs afterward.
why_now: Mercor's $10B valuation (Oct 2025) and reported ~$2B gross run-rate (Jun 2026, lower-tier source, verify) proved frontier labs pay heavily for expert judgment, while contractors complain about pay and lack of protection. Roughly 4M Americans turn 65 each year, and Cerulli projects $124T in transfers through 2048. Postmortem publicity and digital-replica laws are maturing (for example California's 70-year postmortem term). The junior hiring freeze creates a cheap, motivated interviewer pool.
revenue_model: Employer-funded capture sprints at $15-40K per expert (a succession-planning budget line). License revenue share, roughly 40% to expert/estate, 40% to us, 20% to an apprentice pool. Trust administration fee of about 1% of royalties per year. Optional per-client fee from advisors or attorneys who bundle it into estate plans.
non_obvious_insight: The estate, not the living person, is the natural licensor of a lifetime of judgment. Postmortem and IP rights live in probate, and royalty streams fit inheritance planning better than hourly gigs do. Retirees who would never take a gig will happily fund grandchildren with a legacy asset. The demand is a fixed-time resource (a retirement wave) that becomes unavailable once experts are gone.
first_30_days: Pick two narrow, lab-relevant, high-liability trades (for example construction surety adjusters and commercial roofing estimators). Recruit 8-10 retiring experts via trade-association newsletters and five friendly estate attorneys. Pitch each expert's employer a $20K 'retirement capture sprint' as the cash-generating wedge, with licensing rights reserved for the expert's trust. Hire 3 laid-off or junior domain grads as interviewers. Run two pilots. Send redacted sample corpora to 10 human-data teams and vertical AI startups to pre-sell licenses.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.

title: Guardrail Gateway for Law-Firm AI Agents
one_liner: A policy proxy between AI agents and practice-management, billing and trust-accounting systems that enforces ethics rules (trust funds, conflicts, confidentiality) and logs every action for the bar and the insurer.
customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys), the exact segment adopting MCP connectors. Distribution partners are practice-management vendors and malpractice carriers that want to underwrite agent use.
problem: 8am's MyCase MCP connector exposes 73 actions across cases, billing and intake, and 60+ firms adopted it in month one. An agent that can write to billing and trust ledgers can commingle funds, send a privileged detail to the wrong client or email a client without review. Those are disciplinary and malpractice events that no hallucination checker prevents, and solo lawyers have no IT staff, policy or audit trail.
solution: An MCP gateway between Claude, ChatGPT or a 'Firm Agent' and Clio, MyCase and LawPay. Rules block any write touching the trust account without attorney approval by SMS, enforce ethical walls between matters, redact privileged content going to non-approved models, hold outbound client communications for review and rate-limit actions. Every call goes into a tamper-evident log, and a monthly 'agent audit' PDF answers the insurer questionnaire.
why_now: 8am launched its MCP integration in Sep 2026 and says nearly all of its new Firm Agent features already work via MCP, so law-practice data is flowing to third-party agents for the first time. ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024) on generative-AI ethics gives the duties a written source (background, verify).
revenue_model: $79-199/firm/month, carrier-sponsored programs at $10-20 per insured firm per month, and white-label licensing to practice-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The risk from agents is authority (moving money and information), not wrong words. Legal ethics rules are crisp about authority (trust accounting, confidentiality, conflicts), so they compile into policy, unlike 'accuracy'. Distribution will run through practice-management marketplaces, not law-firm websites.
first_30_days: Build the gateway for one platform (Clio or MyCase MCP) with six rules. Recruit 10 small firms through user groups and run it free as a 30-day 'agent audit' that shows near-misses, then convert at $99/month. Take the audit output to two state-bar-affiliated malpractice carriers.

title: Small-Claims Autopilot for Unpaid Invoices
one_liner: Take a solo operator from unpaid invoice to demand letter, filing, service, hearing prep and enforcement in a self-help flow.
customer: Freelancers, contractors and small B2B suppliers with $1k-20k unpaid invoices and no lawyer.
problem: Chasing fails, lawyers cost more than the claim, and small-claims procedure (forms, service, evidence, hearing, enforcement) is confusing, so most owners write off the debt. Cash is tight: nonemployers are less likely to be profitable and lean on personal funds.
solution: Connect invoices, email and texts. The system builds an evidence timeline, verifies the debtor entity and registered agent through state records, drafts a statutory-interest demand letter, files via e-filing where supported, schedules service, and prepares a hearing script and enforcement steps (garnishment and lien templates). It runs as a self-help tool, with a partner attorney for contested cases.
why_now: LLMs read messy invoice and message threads, e-filing is expanding in many courts, and nonemployer cash flow is under stress.
revenue_model: $79 flat per claim plus 10-15% of amounts collected, or a subscription for repeat filers.
non_obvious_insight: The demand letter itself resolves a large share of cases, and enforcement of the judgment is where the value sits, so the product should cover the full path. The regulatory edge is self-help positioning and attorney partners (the FTC's DoNotPay order shows the limits; prior knowledge).
first_30_days: Pick two states with online filing and $10k-plus limits. Run 30 claims for freelancers and trades sourced from community groups, and publish recovery rates and time to payment.

title: Motor-Rewind Shops Become Drone-Motor Cells
one_liner: Qualify a network of existing U.S. electric-motor repair shops to wind and test compliant drone motors with non-Chinese magnets for Drone Dominance suppliers.
customer: Attritable-drone makers and tier-1 subsystem suppliers, including Gauntlet participants and Blue UAS suppliers. They pay per motor (about $60-150, my estimate, versus about $15-30 imported).
problem: The Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program targets more than 200,000 drones by 2027, and about 60,000 are to be ordered from Gauntlet 2 winners. At four motors per quadcopter that is about 240,000 motors for one tranche. China holds about 94% of magnet manufacturing, heavy rare earths stay tight through 2027, and capital is chasing airframes and software, not motors.
solution: Recruit motor-repair shops that already own winding skill, varnish and potting ovens, balancing and hipot test benches. Standardize a 'motor cell kit' (needle winders and fixtures, a single test spec, lot traceability logging) on a lease. The network operator holds customer contracts, source-verified magnet, bearing and lamination supply from domestic vendors, quality paperwork and DPAS-rated order handling, and passes work down. Each shop is audited like a franchisee.
why_now: Gauntlet cadence (roughly every six months) turns motors into a recurring bottleneck, and export controls make compliant sourcing urgent. Motor repair is a slow-shrinking industry, so shops have idle capacity. The Navy is retreating from early-stage funding, so distributed capacity without venture capital is the workable route.
revenue_model: 15-25% operator margin on motor sales, a $15-30k onboarding and equipment-lease fee per shop, and certification renewals. Later expand to ESCs, gimbals and wire harnesses using the same shop network.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is winding know-how and test discipline, not CNC capacity. Motor repair shops are typically classified as repair, so industrial-base maps built from manufacturing codes miss over a thousand of them. Hidden capacity, not new plants, is the fastest path to supply.
first_30_days: Contact regional chapters of the electrical apparatus service association to recruit 5 shops. Get 3 drone makers that currently fly Chinese motors to specify a compliant second-source design. Sell a prototype lot of about 500 motors with customer prepayment and run a first-article test.

title: Contrast Capture: Recovering Iodine From Post-Scan Urine
one_liner: Capture iodinated and gadolinium contrast agents from patients' urine at CT and MRI centers, funded by the drug makers who now owe EU wastewater EPR fees, and recover the iodine and gadolinium.
customer: Contrast-media producers and their EPR schemes (the payer), imaging centers and hospital radiology departments (the host), and water utilities. Start in the Netherlands, Germany, the Nordics and Switzerland.
problem: Contrast agents are excreted almost entirely unchanged within about a day, pass through conventional wastewater treatment, and show up in rivers and drinking water (anthropogenic gadolinium anomalies are documented near large cities). The recast EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive now requires pharma and cosmetics producers to fund at least 80% of quaternary treatment costs. Treating a whole city's effluent for one class of molecule is expensive and contrast agents are very persistent. Meanwhile iodine (tens of grams per contrast CT) and the rare earth gadolinium are supply-concentrated materials being flushed away.
solution: At-source capture in radiology: single-use polymer-lined urine bags or urine-diverting toilets in the imaging suite, handed out at check-out with a prepaid courier or bin for the first voids. A central facility recovers iodine and gadolinium by ion exchange and crystallization and returns them to producers as recycled input. The product sold to producers is 'verified kilograms of contrast removed from the water cycle', a metric their EPR schemes can count against fees. Hospitals get a 'green radiology' certification.
why_now: The recast UWWTD (Directive 2024/3019) is in force and producers are beginning to work out how to meet the 80% cost share, so source-control measures are being sought now. Rare-earth and critical-materials recovery is politically fashionable, giving hospitals and funders a second reason to say yes.
revenue_model: Per-patient capture fee paid by producers or their EPR fund (a few euros per scan), plus sale of recovered iodine and gadolinium (worth roughly $1-3 of iodine per contrast CT, so it supplements rather than carries the business), plus utility co-funding contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The materials are worth pennies to a few dollars per patient; the real revenue is the avoided cost of tertiary and quaternary treatment plants, and the party who owes it is not the hospital but the drug companies. A waste business with a pharma-industry payer.
first_30_days: Sign letters of intent with two imaging centers and one water utility in the Netherlands or Germany. Run a 200-patient pilot with off-the-shelf urine bags and a university lab to measure capture rates and patient compliance. Present the data to the producers' trade body and to the EPR scheme designers as a candidate 'innovative measure' needing pilot funding.

title: Instant Will-Serve Letters From Hydraulic Models
one_liner: Turn a utility's calibrated hydraulic model into a self-serve 'can you serve this address?' oracle that issues fire-flow and will-serve determinations in 48 hours instead of 4 weeks. It starts with developers and sprinkler designers and grows into a water-readiness index for data center and fab site selectors.
customer: Small and mid-size water utilities and the consulting engineering firms that maintain their models are the sellers. The payers are housing developers and fire sprinkler design firms ($250-2,000 per request), then data center, fab and beverage-plant site selection teams ($20-100k per year for the readiness data).
problem: Every subdivision, sprinkler design and industrial hookup needs a will-serve or fire-flow letter. Utilities own a calibrated hydraulic model (WaterGEMS, InfoWater, EPANET), but one or two engineers, or an outside consultant billing $2-8k per run, can operate it. Requests queue for weeks and stall housing and economic development. Worse, the answer 'we have plenty of water' is meaningless. The binding limits are max-day and peak-hour pressure in one pressure zone, fire reserve storage, tank turnover and water age, and the wastewater plant's discharge limits. Big buyers don't know that, and many utilities can't answer within the time a site-selection process allows.
solution: Ingest the utility's model file (.inp or vendor formats) and pre-compute a grid of scenarios. For each node and pressure zone, calculate available fire flow at a 20 psi residual, the maximum added demand before minimum-pressure or velocity limits break, and the effect on tank cycling and water age. Wrap it in a web form and API: enter address, demand, fire-flow requirement, and get a preliminary letter with the utility's letterhead, assumptions and limits. Exceptions go to the utility's licensed engineer for review and stamp. Utilities set the fee and keep most of it. The large-load layer adds wastewater and pretreatment limits, reclaimed-water availability, drought stage and water-rights status. It is published as a 'water hookup readiness' score by utility, like the power-availability maps that data center developers already buy.
why_now: The data center build-out has made water availability a headline and a local permitting fight, and site selection teams already buy power-availability intelligence but have no water equivalent. Housing permitting reform is speeding the approvals that come before utility review, which makes the utility review the bottleneck. Open-source tooling (EPANET and Sandia's WNTR) plus LLM agents that can read model files and draft letters make productizing this feasible for a small team. Many utilities finished models under recent risk-and-resilience assessments and master plans, so the models exist and are unused.
revenue_model: Utility SaaS of $15-40k per year, or free in exchange for a revenue share on developer fees. Per-request fees of $250-2,000 paid by developers, with the utility keeping 50-70%. Data subscriptions of $20-100k per year to site selectors, land brokers and hyperscaler real-estate teams. A consulting-firm channel where the engineering firm resells to its 10-30 utility clients.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not water. It is the one person who is allowed to run the model. The calibrated model is the most valuable unused asset a utility owns, and the answer developers want is hydraulic (peak-day and fire-flow at one node), not a volume in an annual water permit.
first_30_days: Approach one consulting engineering firm that maintains models for 10 or more small utilities and pitch productizing its most repeated task. Build a thin front end on WNTR or EPANET and offer one utility a free pilot: a public fire-flow map plus a letter template. Run the first 20 requests semi-manually, with the engineer generating and signing outputs in the background. Charge local sprinkler design firms $250 per fire-flow letter. Use the results to show turnaround times to two more utilities and to start a data-center-readiness prototype for one region.

title: Robot Gymnasium Inside a Dead Mall
one_liner: Lease dying mall wings for pennies, stage them as real-world sets, and rent them by the day to robotics startups that need diverse places to collect training data.
customer: Humanoid and manipulation-robotics startups (seed to Series B, 20-200 people) and robot-data vendors. They need varied real environments, teleoperator labor and QA'd data, and they can't build a facility of their own.
problem: Robot foundation models are data-starved. Collecting demonstrations needs varied, realistic settings such as grocery aisles, pharmacies, kitchens, hotel corridors, escalators, elevators and glass doors. Lab space in tech metros is tiny and expensive. At-home gig collection is cheap but noisy and raises privacy issues. Chinese players are building 10,000+ m2 collection campuses, and the US has almost nothing comparable.
solution: Take a short-term license on 30-100k sq ft of a dead mall, often at $0.25-1/sq ft because the owner's alternative is a vacant box. Build 8-10 modular sets from closed-store fixtures and thrift furniture: grocery aisle, pharmacy counter, apartment kitchen and bedroom, laundromat, hotel hallway, office. The mall's escalators, revolving doors, elevators, tile and carpet changes and glass storefronts come free as hard perception cases. Sell each set by the day with a motion-capture and camera rig, calibrated lighting and a teleop station. Add a local, trained teleoperator pool billed per accepted demonstration hour, plus a QA pipeline that delivers clean, labeled data.
why_now: Humanoid and VLA robotics funding is in a data-collection race in 2026. MIT Technology Review has covered gig workers training humanoids at home, and China's state-backed training centers run 100+ robots at a time. Paxini reportedly owns a 12,000 m2 collection facility, and AGIBOT rents robots with operators for about $500/day. Dead-mall owners are more distressed than ever, and cheap rental of a robot plus an operator means small teams need somewhere to use them.
revenue_model: Day-rate per environment ($1.5-4k/day). Per-accepted-hour teleop data fees. Monthly reserved 'bays' for resident robotics teams. Later, a revenue share when customers license the resulting datasets.
non_obvious_insight: For robot learning, messy variety with cheap labor and no neighbors matters more than lab polish. A dead mall is free set design, and its owner will pay to have anchor-store fixtures hauled away. The scarce asset is environment diversity plus ops discipline, and the mall itself is nearly free.
first_30_days: Contact 10 owners of dead or dying malls within driving distance of robotics clusters (Pittsburgh, Boston, Detroit, Austin, exurban Bay Area, Atlanta). Sign one 6-month license and build 3 sets for under $25k. Pre-sell 3 pilot collection weeks to startups through robotics meetups and founder networks, with $10-15k deposits. Hire 4 part-time teleoperators and write the data-QA checklist.

title: Cross-Lender Double-Pledge Registry for Receivables
one_liner: A hashed, shared ledger where lenders confirm that an invoice, receivable or auto loan has not already been pledged elsewhere, starting with freight and trade factoring.
customer: Independent factoring companies, ABL desks at regional banks, supply-chain-finance funds and private-credit lenders to mid-market suppliers.
problem: First Brands allegedly double- and triple-pledged about $2.3B of invoices. The SEC charged Tricolor's former CEO and CFO on 18 Aug 2026 with double-pledging subprime auto loans to multiple lenders and securitisations. No single funder can detect overlap because there is no mechanism for lenders to see each other's pledges, so small factors are hit constantly.
solution: Members submit hashed invoice fingerprints (debtor ID, invoice number, amount, date) by API and get 'clean' or 'conflict' back in seconds. Add automated debtor confirmation (email, portal and EDI checks that the invoice exists and where payment is directed) and remittance-diversion alerts. Use private set intersection or salted hashes so lenders never reveal borrowers, and a consortium contract plus UCC-style notice.
why_now: First Brands and Tricolor collapsed in Sept 2025, and DOJ (Jan 2026) and SEC (Aug 2026) actions followed. Private credit's growth, investor demands for collateral verification and bar-association guidance on being 'two-timed' have created board-level urgency.
revenue_model: $0.10-2 per query, $1-5k per month membership for small factors, $50k+ per year for funds, and $5-15 per automated debtor confirmation.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud lives in the gaps between lenders, not inside them. The data everyone needs (each other's pledges) is data nobody will share bilaterally. A neutral registry sells a network effect for detection, like Carfax or the UK's Cifas, rather than a better anomaly detector.
first_30_days: Start with freight factoring, where duplicate invoices and fake brokers are a known problem. Sign 10 independent factors and two fintech ABL lenders through industry associations, build the hashing API, and offer founding members a free tier in exchange for contributing data.

title: Widow's First 90 Days, Sold Through Funeral Homes
one_liner: The pharmacy sees a death first, because refills stop. Package a pharmacist-led medicine cleanup and 90-day check-in program for the surviving spouse, and sell it to funeral homes as their aftercare offering.
customer: Independent funeral homes, which pay $95-195 per family or fold it into a package. Also out-of-town adult children, who pay $29-49 a month for someone local to watch over the surviving parent. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs.
problem: When one spouse dies, the survivor often loses the person who managed the pillbox for both. The survivor skips or double-doses their own meds. The decedent's opioids and benzodiazepines sit in the house, where they can be diverted or swallowed by a grandchild. The first months after spousal loss carry a well-documented spike in illness and mortality, yet the funeral home hands over a grief booklet and the family scatters. No institution owns the medicine cabinet.
solution: A 'Steady' kit enrolled at the arrangement conference with one text. Within a week the pharmacist collects, counts and safely disposes of the decedent's meds, using the pharmacy's DEA-authorized collector status, which funeral homes lack. The pharmacist reconciles the survivor's own meds, resets med sync with adherence packaging and delivery, and flags deprescribing candidates for the doctor. Then come structured 30/60/90-day calls covering eating, sleeping, mood, falls and missed doses, with a report to the adult child and referrals to grief support or the physician when flags trip.
why_now: The first baby boomers turn 80 in 2026, so deaths in the 75-90 cohort will climb for two decades. Small funeral homes are squeezed by cremation and consolidators and need a differentiator beyond price. Independent pharmacies need new cash services as PBM margins collapse. Startups like Empathy have shown that families, employers and insurers pay for post-death help, but none touch medicines. Opioid-settlement money is funding take-back and safe disposal.
revenue_model: Funeral home pays per enrolled family, or the fee is folded into a package uplift. Families or adult children pay a subscription for the 90-day check-in service. The pharmacy earns on med sync, delivery and adherence packaging, plus MTM comprehensive medication review fees. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs pay for bereavement-risk outreach.
non_obvious_insight: A pharmacist learns of a death before the obituary runs, because the refill pattern stops and the survivor's profile changes. The pharmacist and the funeral director are the two professionals in every small town who deal with aging and dying. They have never shared a channel, and a disposal-authorized pharmacist is the only one who can legally take the leftover controlled drugs.
first_30_days: One pharmacy owner recruits two funeral homes in the same county. Build a one-page kit with a DEA-compliant collection procedure, a survivor med review checklist, a med-sync reset and a 30/60/90 call script. Pilot with 20 families, free to the funeral home at first, then $95 per family. Track bottles collected, discrepancies found and 90-day ER visits. Present the case study at the state funeral directors' association meeting and line up an MTM platform partner to bill the comprehensive medication reviews.

title: Telemetry-Underwritten Credit for Defense Sub-Tier Shops
one_liner: Plug low-cost MTConnect adapters into shop CNC machines to create tamper-evident proof of utilization and surge capacity that unlocks equipment loans and rated-order credit lines, and gives primes the capacity data they lack.
customer: 10-50 person machine shops, foundries and sheet-metal shops pursuing defense work (they pay $149-299 a month). Lenders, CDFIs and equipment lessors pay origination fees, and primes and state defense-industrial-base offices later pay for verified-capacity queries.
problem: An industry study finds 'no fit-for-purpose investment model' between R&D and mature production for sub-tier suppliers (castings, forgings, sensors, rocket motors), with VC a sliver and PE putting in only $1-3B a year. Hadrian raised $1.37B while metals robot orders rose just 3% in H1, and shops cannot fund a machine or a cobot cell. Lenders underwrite job shops on tax returns and collateral, and DoD has no real-time data on free spindle-hours.
solution: A hardware-light MTConnect and OPC UA adapter kit and cloud service that logs spindle utilization, part counts, scrap and on-time delivery with signed, tamper-evident records. It issues a 'verified capacity score', lender-ready utilization letters and attestations for DPAS-rated orders, and an anonymized open-capacity feed for primes and government. Partner lenders extend equipment loans and rated-order lines against the score.
why_now: Rated orders, drone and munitions surges and Navy co-investment are pushing demand to sub-tiers just as the Navy stops funding early stages. Publicly funded defense-industrial-base lending vehicles need originators. Modern CNC controls already speak MTConnect, so the marginal hardware cost is small.
revenue_model: $149-299 a month per shop for telemetry and score, 1-2% origination fee from lenders on funded loans, and later a per-query fee from primes and agencies for verified surge capacity.
non_obvious_insight: Utilization telemetry is a better credit signal than a tax return for a job shop, and it doubles as the surge-capacity data the government has never had. The same tamper-evident record serves the lender, the prime and the auditor, so shops pay because it gets them financed.
first_30_days: Partner with a manufacturing extension center and one CDFI or equipment lessor. Install adapters on 10 machines in a defense-heavy cluster (Connecticut or Ohio) and produce the first 3 verified utilization letters to test whether a lender will price better against them.

title: Insurability-at-Close Escrow for Home Listings
one_liner: Listing agents pre-underwrite a house and price the cheapest retrofit fix before listing, so buyers stop discounting for 'uninsurable' uncertainty.
customer: Listing agents, brokerages and sellers in Florida, California and Colorado foothill markets, paying a fee at closing.
problem: Contracts collapse or reprice when buyers cannot get a bindable quote inside the contract window. Homes labeled uninsurable trade to cash buyers at a discount. Much of that discount is uncertainty about fixable issues (roof age, vents, tree clearance), not permanent risk.
solution: A pre-listing 'Insurability File'. Run 3-5 carrier and E&S quotes through a partner agency, then identify the 1-3 cheapest fixes and get contractor quotes. Hold the retrofit cost in escrow at close and give buyers a bindable-quote certificate valid through closing. The buyer gets certainty and the seller gets a closing.
why_now: Citizens has shrunk from about 936K to about 395K policies, so private binding is possible for many Florida homes again. Fannie and Freddie now accept ACV roof coverage (Mar 2026), which opens cheaper insurable paths. Colorado and California rules now credit mitigation.
revenue_model: $750-1,500 per listing at close, plus a 15-25% referral margin on retrofit work and placement commission through the partner agency.
non_obvious_insight: The 'uninsurable' discount is a mispriced-uncertainty premium, and certainty can be bought. Whoever holds the bindable quotes at listing time sets the price.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 top-producing agents in one Colorado or Florida market. Take 10 stuck or repriced listings, build files by hand, and measure price recovery against comps. Then productize the file template.

title: Reverse-Angi: Shops Sell Their Overflow Jobs
one_liner: Missed calls and too-busy jobs get routed to a trusted peer shop that pays the originating shop a referral fee.
customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing and handyman shops with 1-15 techs in one metro, organized in trade circles that already vouch for each other.
problem: About 48% of home-services calls never reach a person (Invoca). Homeowners cite too-busy (21%) and no-response (14%) as barriers to hiring. Angi charges $15-85 per lead that is shared with many bidders, so shops distrust lead-gen. AI receptionists are crowded and merely take messages a shop cannot service.
solution: Shops forward busy, after-hours or out-of-scope calls to a number that answers in seconds, qualifies the job and offers it to the best-matched peer with capacity today. The job is transferred as an exclusive, pre-qualified lead. The originating shop earns a referral share of the invoice and the receiving shop pays a platform fee. Trust comes from peer vouching and network ratings. Cross-trade referrals (plumber to HVAC to electrician) are included.
why_now: In a labor-short market capacity is scarcer than demand: 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects. Lead-gen distrust is high and ServiceTitan is moving upmarket. Real-time voice AI now handles triage well enough to answer instantly.
revenue_model: 20% of transferred-job revenue paid by the receiving shop, split about 10% to the originating shop and 10% to the platform. No subscription, so no adoption friction.
non_obvious_insight: In a labor-short market leads are not scarce, capacity is. Every busy shop is currently throwing away leads, so turn each shop from a lead buyer into a lead seller. It inverts Angi's economics: shops earn money for the calls they cannot take.
first_30_days: Seed 25 shops in one metro through local association groups. Use a Twilio number and a human dispatcher first. Settle via ACH. Track transfers and conversions weekly.

title: Random-Sample CPA Audits of AI Bookkeeping
one_liner: A $79/month independent assurance layer where a licensed CPA reviews a random sample of a micro-business's AI-categorized transactions and signs a monthly accuracy attestation backed by a penalty-reimbursement guarantee.
customer: Nonemployers and 1-10 employee businesses (contractors, salons, restaurants, e-commerce sellers) using AI bookkeeping in QuickBooks, Xero or startup tools. Secondary buyers are AI-bookkeeping vendors wanting white-label certification and lenders wanting attested books.
problem: 46% of AI-using small firms name accuracy as their top problem (Fed SBCS 2026). Intuit and Xero are pushing LLM categorization to millions of users, and Bench's Dec 2024 collapse locked customers out of their books for days. Owners find errors only at a tax bill, a loan denial or a penalty, and new OBBBA reporting (tips and overtime, the $2,000 1099 floor) raises the cost of misclassification.
solution: Stratified sampling weighted toward high-dollar, first-seen-vendor and deduction-sensitive transactions. The CPA confirms against receipts and bank data, fixes errors inside the customer's own software, and issues a monthly signed 'books verified' report with a measured error rate. A small reserve (later insurer-backed) reimburses penalties traceable to verified periods. Every attestation exports to a portable audit file that survives any vendor failing.
why_now: Mass-market LLM bookkeeping arrived in 2026 (Intuit-Anthropic and Xero-Anthropic partnerships) just as CPA headcount stalled near 678K. Intuit cut 17% of staff while opening about 600 offices, which signals that pure-AI trust is unsolved. No incumbent can credibly sell independent assurance on its own output.
revenue_model: $79/month per business with reviewer cost of roughly $15-25/month after AI triage. Add $2-5K/year white-label fees from AI bookkeepers, lender attestation fees, and warranty margin once insurer-backed.
non_obvious_insight: Checking is roughly ten times cheaper than doing, so scarce CPAs can serve 10x more clients as auditors of samples than as preparers. Auditors must be independent of the producer, a position structurally closed to Intuit and Xero. The accumulated error-rate data by tool becomes a Consumer Reports-style asset that the vendors cannot publish themselves.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 part-time or retired CPAs and sign 20 founding clients at $49 from contractor and salon-owner communities. Run a blind test of three AI bookkeepers on 50 anonymized sets of books and publish the error rates for press. Pitch 3 small bookkeeping firms to resell the attestation.

title: Triage Software for Satellite-SOS Rescue Teams
one_liner: Intake, deduplication and dispatch software for county and volunteer search-and-rescue teams flooded by satellite SOS messages.
customer: County sheriff SAR coordinators, state SAR coordinators, national park services and mountain rescue organizations.
problem: As satellite texting reaches ordinary phones, more people go remote and press SOS. Rescuers receive short, delayed, asynchronous messages with weak location data and many false alarms. Coordination centers were built for 911 voice calls, and volunteer teams run on spreadsheets and group texts.
solution: A gateway that ingests SOS relays (email, API, text) from phone makers and satellite messaging providers, deduplicates, geolocates, and adds terrain and weather context. It runs structured 160-character question flows, recommends the resource type to dispatch, and keeps a log for after-action review and cost recovery.
why_now: Satellite messaging on unmodified phones went mainstream across 2025-26 (the briefing shows new carrier launches as late as Sept 28, 2026). AST and SpaceX D2C are scaling, and phone makers are adding satellite SOS. The receiving end has not been rebuilt.
revenue_model: $3-15k per year per county or team. State-level contracts of $50-200k. Optional paid membership or SAR-insurance partnership.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck moved from sending distress to receiving and triaging it. Whoever owns the receive-side workflow becomes the system of record, and public agencies pay for it out of existing rescue budgets.
first_30_days: Shadow three volunteer SAR teams and one state coordinator. Build a minimal intake and dedupe tool that runs alongside their current tools. Offer it free for one summer season in exchange for a paid annual contract.
